newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China talks, hot stocks mark HK handover run-up.
newsitem.headline: China talks, hot stocks mark HK handover run-up.

text.p: A top Chinese official was in Hong Kong on Friday for closed-door talks with the territory's future leader to fine-tune its handover to China in 11 days' time.
On the stock market, meanwhile, "handover euphoria" sent share prices to record highs.

Lu Ping, China's top Hong Kong policy-maker, slipped in on Thursday for discussions with Tung Chee-hwa, a former shipping tycoon who takes the helm on July 1 when the territory becomes a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China.
"They discussed arrangements for the handover ceremony and the ceremony for the establishment of the SAR and the inauguration of the SAR government," a Tung spokesman said.
More than 4,000 VIPs have been invited to the ceremony on the night of June 30 that will mark the end of 156 years of British colonial rule over Hong Kong.

China's decision to hold another ceremony in the early hours of July 1 to swear in an appointed body that will supplant the democratically-elected legislature has prompted the United States and Britain to boycott the inauguration.
Even some pro-China politicians are not entirely in favour of the new legislative arrangements.
Liberal Party leader Allen Lee, who sits in both the existing and post-handover legislatures, said the provisional body lacks credibility because it is not popularly elected.
"The earlier we dissolve this controversy of having the Provisional Legislature the better," Lee told reporters at Hong Kong's Foreign Correspondents' Club on Friday.
But politics seemed to make few ripples on the Hong Kong stock market.
Shares rocketed into record territory, fuelled by rumours a Chinese company would take a stake in Hang Seng Bank Ltd and general enthusiasm over the impending handover, analysts said.
The Hang Seng Index leaped to an all-time high of 15,154.36 points on record turnover of HK$26.6 billion (US$3.44 billion).
"What we are seeing here is definitely handover euphoria coming through here today," said Jake van der Kamp, investment strategist at HG Asia.

The market rally and Lu's visit came as Jimmy McGregor, an architect of Hong Kong's laissez-faire economy and adviser to outgoing Governor Chris Patten, said Beijing would give the territory economic autonomy but never allow political reform.
"China wants this place to continue to be successful, to produce the golden eggs," he said. "The Chinese authorities have no intention of letting Hong Kong develop as a political embarrassment."

But Lu told a local China-funded newspaper that Beijing would maintain Hong Kong's autonomy by stopping anyone from meddling in the territory's affairs or going against its post-handover constitution, the Basic Law.
"We need to play the role of a good 'goalkeeper' to prevent interference in the Special Administrative Region's internal affairs and contravention of the Basic Law," Lu said.
Hong Kong's students, facing doubts about freedom of assembly and expression after China takes over, have pledged to fight on for greater democracy and to adopt a watchdog role.
"We'll continue taking up social responsibilities and be the conscience of society," said Ivy Chan, chairwoman of the pro-democracy Hong Kong Federation of Students.

A political row that stemmed from the People's Liberation Army's first run-in with Hong Kong authorities was just a mixup, the colonial government told a special meeting of the legislature's security panel on Friday.

Miscommunication lay behind an incident when Major-General Zhou Borong, commander of a 200-member advance party of the PLA's Hong Kong garrison, quarrelled with border officers, deputy security chief Carrie Yau told the panel.
"Partly, there is the language problem. Then, it was the first time the chauffeur had driven past the border, and he did not know the procedures," Yau said.
"As for the accusation that Major-General Zhou went through the border without a permit it is not true."
